tagline: A thousand islands barely above the waves
overview:
The Maldives is a chain of about 1,200 coral islands strung across the Indian Ocean southwest of India and Sri Lanka, and only around 200 of them have people living on them. The land adds up to roughly 300 km², about twice the size of Washington, DC, scattered over some 90,000 km² of ocean. It is the flattest country in the world: the highest natural ground rises only about 2.4 meters above sea level.

Around 520,000 people live in the Maldives, nearly all of them Sunni Muslims. Maldivian, also called Dhivehi, is the national language and is written in a script that runs from right to left. The Maldives is a republic. Malé, the capital, is one of the most densely populated cities anywhere, a small island packed edge to edge with buildings. Tourism, with resorts built on their own islands, and tuna fishing support the economy. Because the land is so low, rising seas threaten the country directly.
landAndNature: The Maldives sits on the crest of an undersea mountain ridge, where coral has grown upward over millions of years into ring-shaped atolls; the English word atoll comes from Dhivehi. Each island is a low disc of white coral sand beside a lagoon of astonishing clarity. The reefs shelter more than a thousand fish species, along with manta rays, green turtles and whale sharks, the largest fish in the sea. At night some beaches glow blue where tiny plankton light up in the breaking waves. Warming ocean water has bleached long stretches of coral, and rising seas eat steadily at the islands' edges.
peopleAndCulture: Fish, especially skipjack tuna, is the heart of Maldivian cooking, smoked and dried into hard chips called Maldive fish and stirred into curries, or mixed with coconut, onion and chili into mas huni, eaten with flatbread for breakfast. Boduberu is the best-known music, a circle of drummers and singers building to a fast, pounding finish. The dhoni, a curved wooden boat, has carried Maldivians between islands for centuries. Most islands are small enough to cross on foot in minutes, and children grow up swimming before they can ride a bicycle. Soccer is the favorite sport.
history: Settlers, probably from southern India and Sri Lanka, arrived more than 2,500 years ago, and the islands became a Buddhist kingdom for many centuries. In 1153 the ruler converted to Islam and the country followed. Maldivian cowrie shells were used as money across Asia and Africa, making the islands valuable to traders. Portugal held Malé briefly in the 1500s, and from 1887 the Maldives was a British protectorate while keeping its own sultan. Independence came on July 26, 1965, and the country became a republic in 1968. The Indian Ocean tsunami flooded many islands in 2004. Since then the Maldives has spoken forcefully at world climate talks about rising seas.
funFacts: The Maldives is the flattest country in the world; its highest natural ground is only about 2.4 meters above the sea.
The English word atoll comes from Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives.
In 2009 the Maldivian cabinet held a meeting underwater in scuba gear to draw attention to rising sea levels.
Maldivian cowrie shells were once used as money in markets across Asia and Africa.
Only about 200 of the roughly 1,200 islands are inhabited, and many resorts occupy an entire island each.
